transcript_window.text: So it made sense why people just weren't quite ready yet.

one of the first organizations that I got online was called the New York Civil Liberties Union, which is the New York branch of the ACLU.
And you know, were pretty prominent in New York.
You always heard about them on the news.
They were protecting people's rights, all that kind of stuff.
From there, ball kept rolling.
Word of mouth was spreading.
And Nick's ISP was gaining more more customers.
Within two years, he had outgrown his apartment and had to get a bigger place to hold all the modems and servers he needed.
Over time, it kind morphed or transitioned from like an end user access ISP to more of a hosting kind of an ISP and security consulting ISP.
And by the early 2000s, I wasn't giving individuals the internet access anymore.
I didn't have modems anymore.
had like fiber optic lines and T3 connections and I was hosting these big corporate clients.
you name a few of these corporate clients?

so bigger companies can afford it while the home user doesn't quite, I mean, it was $1 ,000 a month for a T3 back then, right?
